mandarin-clementine.region_label: Utah: St. George Dixie (Mojave-edge high desert)

8.suitability_note_seasoned: St. George's ordinary winter lows of roughly 15 to 20°F (USU Extension Washington County frost data) sit below even mandarin's own low-to-mid 20s°F cold-damage point, so there is no dependable in-ground planting here, and citrus is absent from USU's Washington County Fruits recommendation for this elevation. A container mandarin brought under cover on hard-freeze nights can be kept alive for years and may set some fruit in an unusually mild winter, but this stays protected culture, not a reliable annual harvest.
8.suitability_note_beginner: Mandarin is the toughest common citrus against cold, and St. George winters, with ordinary lows around 15 to 20°F, still get too cold for it outdoors most years. Grow it in a pot you can move under cover on freezing nights. You might get occasional fruit in a mild winter, but do not count on it every year.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: St. George's ordinary winter cold (last frost near March 30, first frost near November 1, USU Extension Washington County) regularly reaches below mandarin's own low-to-mid 20s°F cold-damage point, so an unprotected tree faces a real hard-freeze risk most winters.

mandarin-clementine.region_notes_beginner: Mandarin is the toughest common citrus against cold, but St. George's winters, which drop to ordinary lows around 15 to 20°F, still get too cold for it to live outdoors on its own. Grow it in a container you can bring under cover on the coldest nights, and you may get an occasional harvest in a mild winter, but do not expect a dependable one.
mandarin-clementine.region_notes_seasoned: St. George's zone 8b winters run roughly 15 to 20°F on an ordinary cold night, and USU's Washington County Fruits page, which names the fruits recommended at this elevation, includes no citrus at all. Mandarin, particularly the clementine and satsuma types, is the cold-hardiest common citrus, closer to surviving here than any other, but an ordinary winter night still drops past its own low-to-mid 20s°F damage point. The honest call is a protected container planting, brought under cover on hard-freeze nights, that can live for years and occasionally set fruit in a mild winter rather than a dependable in-ground tree.
mandarin-clementine.cold_basis_seasoned: St. George sits in USDA zone 8b, with ordinary winter lows of roughly 15 to 20°F (USU Extension Washington County frost and elevation data). Mandarin, especially the clementine and satsuma types, is the cold-hardiest common citrus, with mature wood able to take short dips into the low-to-mid 20s°F before real damage, while most other citrus is hurt well above that. Even so, an ordinary St. George winter night still drops past that threshold, and USU's Washington County Fruits page, which lists the fruits recommended at this elevation, names no citrus at all.
mandarin-clementine.cold_basis_beginner: Winters here bring ordinary lows around 15 to 20°F. Mandarin is the toughest common citrus against cold, but that still is not cold enough for it to live outdoors on its own most winters. Grow it in a container you can bring under cover on the coldest nights.
mandarin-clementine.heat_basis_seasoned: St. George summers reach past 100°F in June, July, and August (USU Extension Washington County), plenty of heat to sweeten mandarin fruit in a year the tree does set. Winter cold, not summer heat, is what keeps mandarin to a protected container planting here.
mandarin-clementine.heat_basis_beginner: Our summers here are plenty hot for mandarin fruit to taste good. Winter cold, not a lack of summer warmth, is why this is not a reliable outdoor tree.

lemon.region_label: Utah: St. George Dixie (Mojave-edge high desert)

8.suitability_note_seasoned: St. George's ordinary winter lows of roughly 15 to 20°F (USU Extension Washington County frost data) are well past true lemon's high-20s°F damage point and still edge past Meyer lemon's own low-to-mid 20s°F cold tolerance, so there is no dependable in-ground planting here, and citrus is absent from USU's Washington County Fruits recommendation for this elevation. A container Meyer lemon, brought under cover on hard-freeze nights, can be kept alive for years and may set some fruit in an unusually mild winter; true lemon is too tender to attempt outdoors here at all.
8.suitability_note_beginner: Regular lemon is too tender for St. George's winters, which drop to ordinary lows around 15 to 20°F. The hardier Meyer lemon, bred for cold-marginal climates, does a bit better and can survive for years in a container you bring under cover on freezing nights, but do not expect a reliable harvest even from it.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: St. George's ordinary winter cold (last frost near March 30, first frost near November 1, USU Extension Washington County) reaches well past true lemon's high-20s°F damage point and edges past even Meyer lemon's low-to-mid 20s°F tolerance, so hard-freeze nights are a real risk for an unprotected tree most winters.

lemon.region_notes_beginner: Regular lemon does not work outdoors in St. George; winters here, with ordinary lows around 15 to 20°F, are too much for it. The hardier Meyer lemon, bred for cold-marginal gardens, can survive for years in a container brought under cover on freezing nights, and may give you fruit in an unusually mild winter, but do not count on a dependable harvest.
lemon.region_notes_seasoned: St. George's zone 8b winters run roughly 15 to 20°F on an ordinary cold night, and USU's Washington County Fruits page, which names the fruits recommended at this elevation, includes no citrus at all. True lemon is damaged in the high 20s°F and is not a realistic outdoor choice here. Meyer lemon, a lemon by mandarin hybrid bred for marginal climates, tolerates cold into the low-to-mid 20s°F, closer to St. George's winter low but still not clearing it reliably. The honest call is a protected container Meyer, brought under cover on hard-freeze nights, that can live for years and occasionally set fruit in a mild winter.
lemon.cold_basis_seasoned: St. George sits in USDA zone 8b, with ordinary winter lows of roughly 15 to 20°F (USU Extension Washington County frost and elevation data). True lemon (Eureka, Lisbon) is damaged in the high 20s°F, well above that band; the hardier Meyer lemon, a lemon by mandarin hybrid bred for cold-marginal climates, tolerates cold into the low-to-mid 20s°F, still short of St. George's ordinary winter low. USU's Washington County Fruits page, which lists the fruits recommended at this elevation, names no citrus at all.
lemon.cold_basis_beginner: Winters here bring ordinary lows around 15 to 20°F. Regular lemon is too tender for that outright; even the hardier Meyer lemon, bred for cold-marginal gardens, cannot reliably take it either. Grow Meyer lemon in a container you bring under cover on the coldest nights, and skip regular lemon outdoors altogether.

orange-navel.region_label: Utah: St. George Dixie (Mojave-edge high desert)

8.suitability_note_seasoned: St. George's ordinary winter lows of roughly 15 to 20°F (USU Extension Washington County frost data) sit well past navel orange's mid-20s°F wood-damage point and its roughly 26°F fruit-freeze point, and citrus is absent from USU's Washington County Fruits recommendation for this elevation. There is no dependable in-ground or even long-term container option here; grow it, if at all, as a fully enclosed greenhouse or indoor specimen rather than a garden planting.
8.suitability_note_beginner: Winters here, with ordinary lows around 15 to 20°F, regularly drop past the point that damages both the tree and the fruit of a navel orange. Unlike lemon or mandarin, there is no cold-hardy orange type to fall back on, so this is not a realistic tree to try outdoors, even in a container, in St. George.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: St. George's ordinary winter cold (last frost near March 30, first frost near November 1, USU Extension Washington County) is a hard freeze past navel orange's own mid-20s°F wood-damage point in most years.

orange-navel.region_notes_beginner: Navel orange does not work outdoors in St. George. Winters here, with ordinary lows around 15 to 20°F, regularly damage both the tree and the fruit, and unlike lemon or mandarin there is no cold-hardy orange type to make it work in a container either.
orange-navel.region_notes_seasoned: St. George's zone 8b winters run roughly 15 to 20°F on an ordinary cold night, well past navel orange's mid-20s°F wood-damage point and roughly 26°F fruit-freeze point. USU's Washington County Fruits page, which names the fruits recommended at this elevation, includes no citrus at all, and unlike lemon (Meyer) or mandarin (clementine, satsuma), navel orange has no widely grown cold-hardy selection to close the gap. Summer heat is not the problem, St. George easily clears 100°F in June, July, and August, but winter cold decides the case here.
orange-navel.cold_basis_seasoned: St. George sits in USDA zone 8b, with ordinary winter lows of roughly 15 to 20°F (USU Extension Washington County frost and elevation data). Navel orange takes wood damage near the mid-20s°F and fruit damage near 26°F, both well above St. George's ordinary winter low, and unlike mandarin or lemon it has no widely available cold-hardy selection to close that gap. USU's Washington County Fruits page, which lists the fruits recommended at this elevation, names no citrus at all.
orange-navel.cold_basis_beginner: Winters here bring ordinary lows around 15 to 20°F, well past the point that damages both the wood and the fruit of a navel orange tree. There is no cold-hardy orange type the way there is for lemon or mandarin, so this is not a realistic outdoor tree here.
orange-navel.heat_basis_seasoned: St. George summers reach past 100°F in June, July, and August (USU Extension Washington County), more than enough heat to sweeten navel orange fruit if the tree could clear winter. Winter cold, not summer heat, rules this crop out here.
orange-navel.heat_basis_beginner: Our summers here are plenty hot for orange fruit to taste good. Winter cold is the reason this does not work outdoors in St. George, not a lack of summer warmth.

lime.region_label: Utah: St. George Dixie (Mojave-edge high desert)

8.suitability_note_seasoned: St. George's ordinary winter lows of roughly 15 to 20°F (USU Extension Washington County frost data) are far past lime's own freezing-point damage threshold, the most cold-sensitive of the common citrus, and citrus is absent altogether from USU's Washington County Fruits recommendation for this elevation. There is no dependable outdoor or long-term container option here; a lime tree needs full indoor housing through the cold season to survive at all.
8.suitability_note_beginner: Lime is hurt by cold more easily than any other common citrus, damaged practically at the freezing point, and St. George winters, with ordinary lows around 15 to 20°F, regularly drop well below that. This is not a realistic tree to try outdoors here, even in a container brought in only on cold nights; it needs to live indoors through winter.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: St. George's ordinary winter cold (last frost near March 30, first frost near November 1, USU Extension Washington County) is a hard freeze far past lime's own freezing-point damage threshold, the most cold-sensitive of the common citrus.

lime.region_notes_beginner: Lime does not work outdoors in St. George. It is hurt by cold more easily than any other common citrus, damaged practically at freezing, and winters here, with ordinary lows around 15 to 20°F, regularly drop well below that.
lime.region_notes_seasoned: St. George's zone 8b winters run roughly 15 to 20°F on an ordinary cold night, far past lime's own freezing-point damage threshold, the most cold-sensitive of the common citrus and one with no hardy selection comparable to Meyer lemon or clementine mandarin. USU's Washington County Fruits page, which names the fruits recommended at this elevation, includes no citrus at all. A lime here needs full indoor housing through the cold season; there is no honest outdoor or seasonal-container call to make.
lime.cold_basis_seasoned: St. George sits in USDA zone 8b, with ordinary winter lows of roughly 15 to 20°F (USU Extension Washington County frost and elevation data). Lime is the least cold-tolerant common citrus, damaged at or near the freezing point itself, and has no cold-hardy selection comparable to Meyer lemon or clementine mandarin. USU's Washington County Fruits page, which lists the fruits recommended at this elevation, names no citrus at all.
lime.cold_basis_beginner: Winters here bring ordinary lows around 15 to 20°F, far past the point where lime, the most cold-sensitive common citrus, takes damage right around freezing. There is no hardy lime type to fall back on, so this is not a realistic outdoor tree here.

8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: St. George's ordinary winter cold (last frost near March 30, first frost near November 1, USU Extension Washington County) is a hard freeze past grapefruit's own mid-20s°F wood-damage point in most years.

grapefruit.region_notes_beginner: Grapefruit does not work outdoors in St. George. Winters here, with ordinary lows around 15 to 20°F, regularly damage both the tree and the fruit, and unlike lemon or mandarin there is no cold-hardy grapefruit type to make it work in a container either.
grapefruit.region_notes_seasoned: St. George's zone 8b winters run roughly 15 to 20°F on an ordinary cold night, well past grapefruit's mid-20s°F wood- and fruit-damage point. grapefruit.cold_basis_beginner: Winters here bring ordinary lows around 15 to 20°F, well past the point that damages both the wood and the fruit of a grapefruit tree. There is no cold-hardy grapefruit type to fall back on, so this is not a realistic outdoor tree here.
grapefruit.heat_basis_seasoned: St. George summers reach past 100°F in June, July, and August (USU Extension Washington County), more than enough heat for grapefruit, the citrus with the highest summer-heat need, to sweeten its fruit if the tree could clear winter. grapefruit.heat_basis_beginner: Our summers here are plenty hot for grapefruit. Winter cold, not summer heat, is why this does not work outdoors in St. George.
